blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that for independent observations from a population with mean μ and finite variance σ², the sampling distribution of x̄ approaches a Normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n as n increases, whatever the shape of the population distribution. Equivalently, (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ/√n) approaches the standard Normal distribution (recall §5.7.2.2.1).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: §6.5 fixed the centre (μ) and spread (σ/√n) of the sampling distribution of x̄. The CLT adds its shape: approximately Normal, even when individual values are skewed or bimodal. This is why the Normal distribution matters so much in the rest of the book. It is not that most raw variables are Normal (many are not); it is that means of almost anything become approximately Normal. The binomial’s approach to a Normal shape for large n (recall §5.7.1.2) is one case of it, since a binomial count is a sum of independent 0/1 values.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Hospital length of stay is right-skewed (recall §3.9): most stays are short, a few are very long. Draw repeated samples of 40 patients and compute each sample’s mean stay. The histogram of those means is roughly bell-shaped and centred on the population mean, although the individual stays are heavily skewed.

points.html: The CLT is about the sampling distribution of the mean (or a sum). It does not say that raw data become Normal in large samples.

How large is large enough? A convention, not a law: n ≥ 30 is widely used as the point where the Normal approximation for a mean is adequate (Kwak & Kim, 2017). The exception: strongly skewed or heavy-tailed populations need larger samples, and for a proportion the check is on the expected counts, np and n(1 − p) (recall §5.7.2.2.4), not on n alone.
Independence matters. For clustered samples the CLT applies to cluster-level summaries, and the effective sample size (§6.2.6), not the raw count, governs how good the approximation is.

blocks.html: Implications of the Central Limit Theorem

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A statistical method is robust to non-normality when its stated error rates (for example, 95% coverage of a confidence interval) stay approximately correct even though the data are not Normal. The CLT is what makes methods built on means robust in this sense when samples are large enough.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Many methods in later chapters (the t-test, ANOVA, confidence intervals for means) are derived assuming Normal data. What they actually need is a Normal sampling distribution of the mean, and the CLT supplies that for moderately large n even when individual values are skewed.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Haemoglobin may be mildly skewed in a population. A 95% confidence interval for the mean haemoglobin, built on the Normal or t-distribution (recall §5.7.2.3; the interval itself is §7.2.1), is still valid for a sample of reasonable size, because the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately Normal even though individual readings are not.

points.html: Proportions and sums: a sample proportion is the mean of 0/1 values, so the CLT covers proportions too. This is the basis of the Normal-approximation confidence interval for a proportion (§7.2.2).

The limit of robustness: with small samples from strongly skewed data, the Normal approximation can mislead. Non-parametric methods (Chapter 10) and exact or bootstrap intervals (§7.2.4) are the fallback.
